tagline: Across the Cascades, a highway reshaped by a pass and a reservoir
intro: The White Pass Scenic Byway winds through river valleys and forests, climbing from foothills near Interstate 5 toward the Cascades before descending to the open country of the Yakima Valley. State of Washington Tourism gives the Marys Corner-to-Naches drive as 124 miles and three hours. Designated a National Scenic Byway in 2009, it offers lakes, rivers and scenic pullouts in the tourism office’s account. The high crossing is 4,500-foot White Pass, south of Mount Rainier.

The state legislature added a White Pass shortcut between Packwood and Naches to the highway system in 1931. The White Pass Highway opened in August 1951, making a shortcut between southwest Washington and Yakima. The US 12 designation followed in 1967. That December, dam construction forced the road onto a new 16-mile route through Morton, ahead of the reservoir that would flood parts of the Cowlitz valley.

US 12 leaves I-5 south of Napavine and follows the Cowlitz River east toward Mossyrock. Heading east, Mossyrock sits between Mayfield and Riffe lakes, followed by the timber town of Morton. Randle and Packwood lead toward White Pass; Packwood lies along the Cowlitz River. Beyond the pass, the route descends toward Naches, where orchards and rolling hills mark the eastern gateway.

moments.title: Riffe Lake
moments.text: Riffe Lake covers the sites of Kosmos, Nesika and Riffe, whose residents relocated before the planned flooding. Tacoma City Light created the reservoir with Mossyrock Dam in 1968. At Kosmos, logging, sawmills and mercury mining had supported the town. Contractors razed most buildings, leaving their foundations. Tacoma Power lowered the lake’s maximum level by 30 feet in 2017 because of earthquake concerns involving the dam’s spillway piers. At low water, remnants of the former communities can be seen. The reservoir’s official name changed from Davisson Lake to Riffe Lake in 1976 after Lewis County residents petitioned for a local name.

moments.title: Morton
moments.text: The White Pass Highway’s move through Morton in December 1967 put the road through a town already shaped by timber. Logging was one of its early sources of revenue, alongside harvesting cascara bark and mining cinnabar, the ore of mercury. In the 1950s Morton was known as the “tie mill capital of the world.” The historic train depot provides a present connection to that railroad history, and State of Washington Tourism includes it among the town’s attractions. The Loggers’ Jubilee continues the town’s logging contests as part of a weekend celebration.

moments.title: White Pass
moments.text: The highway crosses the Cascades at 4,500 feet, linking Lewis County on the west with Yakima County on the east. The pass takes its name from Charles A. White, who led a Northern Pacific Railroad survey party here in 1878. A road crossing between Packwood and Naches entered the state highway system in 1931; the link was completed in August 1951. White Pass Ski Area opened at the summit in January 1953. Ski racing twins Phil and Steve Mahre grew up here while their father Dave managed the mountain. The crossing lies southeast of Mount Rainier and north of Goat Rocks.

practical: White Pass: White Pass is an all-season highway, typically open year-round, but heavy winter snow can close it temporarily. (checked 2026-10-11)
